case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old man with insidious onset of limited mobility of joints visited our clinic for evaluation. Six months prior, he found his palms could not make full contact with each other (the “prayer sign”). He had not been able to fully clench his fists for 2 months or squat for the past 10 days. No erythema, edema, or sclerotic skin plaque had been found on his limbs or trunk. No Raynaud phenomenon had occurred. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, he showed bilateral limited mobility of interphalangeal (hands), metacarpophalangeal, wrist, interphalangeal (feet), metatarsophalangeal, and ankle joints (Video). No muscular atrophy or sclerodactyly was found. The prayer sign (Figure 1A) and the “groove sign” (Figure 1B) were observed. Blood test results indicated eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count, 1300 μL; reference, <500μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, 31 mm/h; reference, <15 mm/h) and C-reactive protein (CRP, 3.01 mg/dL; reference, <0.8 mg/dL [to convert to mg/L, multiply by 10]). Liver and kidney function tests, creatine kinase level, electrolyte level, thyroid function, globulin concentration, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) level were unremarkable. Electrocardiogram, cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging, and plain radiographs of hands, wrists, feet, and ankles were normal. Nerve conduction studies performed in all 4 limbs were normal. Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous activities in muscles of limbs, including fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves (1+ or 2+). Myotonic discharges were seen in bilateral extensor digitorum.
case_info.caption: A, The patient’s bilateral palms and fingers could not make full contact due to the limited mobility of interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints. B, Linear depression (arrowheads) was seen along the course of superficial vein when limb was elevated.
case_info.explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. There were moderate variations in muscle fiber size. Some muscle fibers were atrophic. A scatter of necrotic muscle fibers was seen. The myositis, which is frequently observed in EF, may explain the EMG findings in this patient, as myotonic discharges may be seen in a number of acquired myopathic disorders, including myositis.1Also, certain drugs (eg, statins) can cause myotonic discharges.1The clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of EF. The etiology and exact incidence of EF remain unknown. A variety of etiological factors have been proposed, such as strenuous exercise or trauma preceding disease onset.8To our knowledge, no randomized trials have evaluated therapies for EF. Usually, treatment is started with systemic glucocorticoids at doses equivalent to prednisone, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day.8Concomitant immunosuppressants (eg, methotrexate) are used by some practitioners as the initial therapy or when patients are steroid resistant or refractory.8,9For this patient, prednisone and cyclophosphamide were prescribed. Nine months later, his joint mobility was improved. Diagnosing EF is challenging because of its rarity. Bilaterally limited mobility of joints, cutaneous manifestations (eg, groove sign and orange peel appearance), and peripheral eosinophilia are useful clues to the diagnosis of EF.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

A 31-year-old man with insidious onset of limited mobility of joints visited our clinic for evaluation. Six months prior, he found his palms could not make full contact with each other (the “prayer sign”). He had not been able to fully clench his fists for 2 months or squat for the past 10 days. No erythema, edema, or sclerotic skin plaque had been found on his limbs or trunk. No Raynaud phenomenon had occurred. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, he showed bilateral limited mobility of interphalangeal (hands), metacarpophalangeal, wrist, interphalangeal (feet), metatarsophalangeal, and ankle joints (Video). Liver and kidney function tests, creatine kinase level, electrolyte level, thyroid function, globulin concentration, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) level were unremarkable. Electrocardiogram, cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging, and plain radiographs of hands, wrists, feet, and ankles were normal. Nerve conduction studies performed in all 4 limbs were normal. Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous activities in muscles of limbs, including fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves (1+ or 2+). Myotonic discharges were seen in bilateral extensor digitorum.

case_info.explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. There were moderate variations in muscle fiber size. Some muscle fibers were atrophic. A scatter of necrotic muscle fibers was seen. The myositis, which is frequently observed in EF, may explain the EMG findings in this patient, as myotonic discharges may be seen in a number of acquired myopathic disorders, including myositis.1Also, certain drugs (eg, statins) can cause myotonic discharges.1The clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of EF. The etiology and exact incidence of EF remain unknown. A variety of etiological factors have been proposed, such as strenuous exercise or trauma preceding disease onset.8To our knowledge, no randomized trials have evaluated therapies for EF. Usually, treatment is started with systemic glucocorticoids at doses equivalent to prednisone, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day.8Concomitant immunosuppressants (eg, methotrexate) are used by some practitioners as the initial therapy or when patients are steroid resistant or refractory.8,9For this patient, prednisone and cyclophosphamide were prescribed. Nine months later, his joint mobility was improved. Diagnosing EF is challenging because of its rarity. Bilaterally limited mobility of joints, cutaneous manifestations (eg, groove sign and orange peel appearance), and peripheral eosinophilia are useful clues to the diagnosis of EF.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

case_info.explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. There were moderate variations in muscle fiber size. Some muscle fibers were atrophic. A scatter of necrotic muscle fibers was seen. The myositis, which is frequently observed in EF, may explain the EMG findings in this patient, as myotonic discharges may be seen in a number of acquired myopathic disorders, including myositis.1Also, certain drugs (eg, statins) can cause myotonic discharges.1The clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of EF. The etiology and exact incidence of EF remain unknown. A variety of etiological factors have been proposed, such as strenuous exercise or trauma preceding disease onset.8To our knowledge, no randomized trials have evaluated therapies for EF. Usually, treatment is started with systemic glucocorticoids at doses equivalent to prednisone, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day.8Concomitant immunosuppressants (eg, methotrexate) are used by some practitioners as the initial therapy or when patients are steroid resistant or refractory.8,9For this patient, prednisone and cyclophosphamide were prescribed. Nine months later, his joint mobility was improved. Diagnosing EF is challenging because of its rarity. Bilaterally limited mobility of joints, cutaneous manifestations (eg, groove sign and orange peel appearance), and peripheral eosinophilia are useful clues to the diagnosis of EF.

case_info.explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. case_info.explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. There were moderate variations in muscle fiber size. Some muscle fibers were atrophic. A scatter of necrotic muscle fibers was seen. The myositis, which is frequently observed in EF, may explain the EMG findings in this patient, as myotonic discharges may be seen in a number of acquired myopathic disorders, including myositis.1Also, certain drugs (eg, statins) can cause myotonic discharges.1The clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of EF. The etiology and exact incidence of EF remain unknown. A variety of etiological factors have been proposed, such as strenuous exercise or trauma preceding disease onset.8To our knowledge, no randomized trials have evaluated therapies for EF. Usually, treatment is started with systemic glucocorticoids at doses equivalent to prednisone, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day.8Concomitant immunosuppressants (eg, methotrexate) are used by some practitioners as the initial therapy or when patients are steroid resistant or refractory.8,9For this patient, prednisone and cyclophosphamide were prescribed. Nine months later, his joint mobility was improved. Diagnosing EF is challenging because of its rarity. Bilaterally limited mobility of joints, cutaneous manifestations (eg, groove sign and orange peel appearance), and peripheral eosinophilia are useful clues to the diagnosis of EF.

Six months prior, he found his palms could not make full contact with each other (the “prayer sign”). He had not been able to fully clench his fists for 2 months or squat for the past 10 days. No erythema, edema, or sclerotic skin plaque had been found on his limbs or trunk. No Raynaud phenomenon had occurred. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, he showed bilateral limited mobility of interphalangeal (hands), metacarpophalangeal, wrist, interphalangeal (feet), metatarsophalangeal, and ankle joints (Video). No muscular atrophy or sclerodactyly was found. The prayer sign (Figure 1A) and the “groove sign” (Figure 1B) were observed. Blood test results indicated eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count, 1300 μL; reference, <500μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, 31 mm/h; reference, <15 mm/h) and C-reactive protein (CRP, 3.01 mg/dL; reference, <0.8 mg/dL [to convert to mg/L, multiply by 10]). Liver and kidney function tests, creatine kinase level, electrolyte level, thyroid function, globulin concentration, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) level were unremarkable. Electrocardiogram, cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging, and plain radiographs of hands, wrists, feet, and ankles were normal. Nerve conduction studies performed in all 4 limbs were normal. Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous activities in muscles of limbs, including fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves (1+ or 2+). Myotonic discharges were seen in bilateral extensor digitorum.

case_info.explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. There were moderate variations in muscle fiber size. Some muscle fibers were atrophic. A scatter of necrotic muscle fibers was seen. The myositis, which is frequently observed in EF, may explain the EMG findings in this patient, as myotonic discharges may be seen in a number of acquired myopathic disorders, including myositis.1Also, certain drugs (eg, statins) can cause myotonic discharges.1The clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of EF. The etiology and exact incidence of EF remain unknown. A variety of etiological factors have been proposed, such as strenuous exercise or trauma preceding disease onset.8To our knowledge, no randomized trials have evaluated therapies for EF. Usually, treatment is started with systemic glucocorticoids at doses equivalent to prednisone, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day.8Concomitant immunosuppressants (eg, methotrexate) are used by some practitioners as the initial therapy or when patients are steroid resistant or refractory.8,9For this patient, prednisone and cyclophosphamide were prescribed. Nine months later, his joint mobility was improved. Diagnosing EF is challenging because of its rarity. Bilaterally limited mobility of joints, cutaneous manifestations (eg, groove sign and orange peel appearance), and peripheral eosinophilia are useful clues to the diagnosis of EF.

case_info.explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. There were moderate variations in muscle fiber size. Some muscle fibers were atrophic. A scatter of necrotic muscle fibers was seen. The myositis, which is frequently observed in EF, may explain the EMG findings in this patient, as myotonic discharges may be seen in a number of acquired myopathic disorders, including myositis.1Also, certain drugs (eg, statins) can cause myotonic discharges.1The clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of EF. The etiology and exact incidence of EF remain unknown. A variety of etiological factors have been proposed, such as strenuous exercise or trauma preceding disease onset.8To our knowledge, no randomized trials have evaluated therapies for EF. Usually, treatment is started with systemic glucocorticoids at doses equivalent to prednisone, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day.8Concomitant immunosuppressants (eg, methotrexate) are used by some practitioners as the initial therapy or when patients are steroid resistant or refractory.8,9For this patient, prednisone and cyclophosphamide were prescribed. Nine months later, his joint mobility was improved. Diagnosing EF is challenging because of its rarity. Bilaterally limited mobility of joints, cutaneous manifestations (eg, groove sign and orange peel appearance), and peripheral eosinophilia are useful clues to the diagnosis of EF.

case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old man with insidious onset of limited mobility of joints visited our clinic for evaluation. Six months prior, he found his palms could not make full contact with each other (the “prayer sign”). He had not been able to fully clench his fists for 2 months or squat for the past 10 days. No erythema, edema, or sclerotic skin plaque had been found on his limbs or trunk. No Raynaud phenomenon had occurred. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, he showed bilateral limited mobility of interphalangeal (hands), metacarpophalangeal, wrist, interphalangeal (feet), metatarsophalangeal, and ankle joints (Video). No muscular atrophy or sclerodactyly was found. The prayer sign (Figure 1A) and the “groove sign” (Figure 1B) were observed. Blood test results indicated eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count, 1300 μL; reference, <500μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, 31 mm/h; reference, <15 mm/h) and C-reactive protein (CRP, 3.01 mg/dL; reference, <0.8 mg/dL [to convert to mg/L, multiply by 10]). Liver and kidney function tests, creatine kinase level, electrolyte level, thyroid function, globulin concentration, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) level were unremarkable. Electrocardiogram, cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging, and plain radiographs of hands, wrists, feet, and ankles were normal. Nerve conduction studies performed in all 4 limbs were normal. Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous activities in muscles of limbs, including fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves (1+ or 2+). Myotonic discharges were seen in bilateral extensor digitorum.

case_info.explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. There were moderate variations in muscle fiber size. Some muscle fibers were atrophic. A scatter of necrotic muscle fibers was seen. The myositis, which is frequently observed in EF, may explain the EMG findings in this patient, as myotonic discharges may be seen in a number of acquired myopathic disorders, including myositis.1Also, certain drugs (eg, statins) can cause myotonic discharges.1The clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of EF. The etiology and exact incidence of EF remain unknown. A variety of etiological factors have been proposed, such as strenuous exercise or trauma preceding disease onset.8To our knowledge, no randomized trials have evaluated therapies for EF. Usually, treatment is started with systemic glucocorticoids at doses equivalent to prednisone, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day.8Concomitant immunosuppressants (eg, methotrexate) are used by some practitioners as the initial therapy or when patients are steroid resistant or refractory.8,9For this patient, prednisone and cyclophosphamide were prescribed. Nine months later, his joint mobility was improved. Diagnosing EF is challenging because of its rarity. Bilaterally limited mobility of joints, cutaneous manifestations (eg, groove sign and orange peel appearance), and peripheral eosinophilia are useful clues to the diagnosis of EF.
